analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for workers to prove job discrimination and win real damages.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 272–154, but the Senate never enacted it, and no version of the civil rights bill became law in 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: Responding to a string of 1989 Supreme Court decisions that cut back job-discrimination protections, this bill would have shifted the burden of proof so employers had to justify practices with racially or sexually skewed effects as business necessities, doubled the deadline to file a complaint from 180 days to two years, and let victims of intentional discrimination win compensatory and punitive damages with a jury trial. The House passed it 272–154 in August 1990, but the Senate never enacted a final bill before that Congress ended; a softened version with most of the same provisions became law in 1991.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face discrimination on the job — women, racial and ethnic minorities, religious minorities, and older workers — would find it easier to prove discrimination, would have two years instead of 180 days to file, and could win compensatory and punitive damages, jury trials, and attorney's fees including expert costs. Federal employees would get the same interest on delayed back pay as private parties and more time to sue.

how_it_helps.text: Once a worker shows an employment practice has a disparate impact by race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, the employer would have to prove the practice is required by business necessity — restoring the rule the Supreme Court had weakened in 1989.
Discrimination need only be one motivating factor for an employment decision, not the sole reason, making it easier to win mixed-motive cases.

Victims of intentional discrimination could recover compensatory damages and — where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference — punitive damages, with the right to a jury trial; the House-passed version limited these to intentional-discrimination claims and set a cap on punitive damages.

The deadline to file a discrimination charge would double from 180 days to two years, and federal employees would get 90 days instead of 30 to sue and the same interest on delayed payment as private parties.

Attorney's-fee awards would include expert fees and other litigation expenses, and a seniority system written into a union contract with intent to discriminate could be challenged while the contract is in force.
The bill would restore the full right to make and enforce contracts under 42 U.S.C. 1981, reversing a 1989 ruling that had narrowed it.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — businesses and unions named as respondents — would bear the cost: more lawsuits, jury trials, compensatory and punitive damage awards in intentional-discrimination cases, expert and attorney's fees when they lose, and the obligation to justify or replace practices with skewed effects. The federal government would pay interest on delayed awards to its own employees.

drawbacks.text: Business groups warned the burden-of-proof shift would push employers toward hiring by the numbers; the House-passed version responded by stating that a statistical imbalance alone proves nothing, limiting damages to intentional discrimination, and capping punitive damages.
The bill raised the cost of doing business: employers could face jury trials, punitive damages, a two-year window for old claims, and revived challenges to seniority systems in union contracts.

The House-passed version would let courts strike down even a practice shown to be a business necessity if a less discriminatory alternative 'would serve the respondent as well' — a standard critics said was vague and would invite litigation over what counts as equally good.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits were concrete — real money damages, a workable filing window, and a burden of proof that matches how employment practices actually work — and its costs fell on employers as litigation exposure, which is how anti-discrimination law is supposed to deter violations. The House-passed version already contained the main compromises business critics demanded (no liability from statistics alone, damages limited to intentional discrimination, a punitive-damage cap), so the design debate was narrower than the fight over it suggested. The bill failed for political reasons, not because it was badly built; most of it became law a year later in softened form in the Civil Rights Act of 1991.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 272–154, then set it aside in favor of the Senate's companion bill, which died after Republican senators blocked it from a final vote while President George H.W. Bush threatened a veto — so no civil rights law passed in 1990.

narrative.text: Congress wrote the bill in direct response to 1989 Supreme Court decisions that, in its own findings, 'cut back dramatically on the scope and effectiveness of civil rights protections' and left remedies 'not adequate to deter unlawful discrimination.'

The bill was referred jointly to the Education and Labor and Judiciary Committees, went through months of hearings and markups, and was reported in amended form — the Judiciary Committee reporting it adversely while the Rules Committee set up a substitute text for floor action.
On August 3, 1990, the House passed the amended bill 272–154, with 240 of 256 voting Democrats in favor and 142 of 176 voting Republicans opposed; a Republican motion to recommit failed.
Immediately on passage, the House laid H.R. 4000 on the table in favor of the Senate companion, S. 2104, making the Senate bill the vehicle.

The Senate never enacted a final bill: President Bush denounced it as a 'quota bill' and threatened a veto, Senate Republicans talked the companion bill to death, and a procedural vote to cut off debate fell short in October 1990 — leaving the 1989 court rulings in place for that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced the new damages, jury trials, and burden-of-proof rules were spared for that Congress; workers lost out in 1990 but got most of the same provisions a year later in the narrower Civil Rights Act of 1991, which President Bush signed.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split sharply by party — 240 Democrats to 12 for the bill, 32 Republicans to 142 against — and the bill died in the Senate over unified Republican opposition under a Republican president's veto threat.

industries.note: The bill would raise employer exposure to discrimination suits through new compensatory and punitive damages, jury trials, a two-year filing window, and a burden of proof that forces employers to justify practices with skewed effects. That cost is precisely the deterrent on workers' behalf, so the industry's interest runs against the public's here.

Fee awards would now cover expert fees and litigation expenses, and more claims would survive, meaning more viable cases for lawyers who represent discrimination plaintiffs. Their financial interest in stronger enforcement lines up with workers' interests.

Union members gain from stronger discrimination remedies, but the bill lets discriminatory seniority systems written into collective bargaining agreements be challenged while the contract is in force, exposing unions and employers as respondents.
